extracted.intended_audience: students, clergy, and readers of theology and political philosophy interested in church–state relations and ecclesiastical authority
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the nature and limits of ecclesiastical power: what apostles and ministers are commissioned to do (preach, teach, baptize, bind/loose), the meaning and effects of sacraments and excommunication, criteria for martyrdom, and relations between Church and civil rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers' power limited to proclamation and persuasion, not coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no Coercive Power left them by our Saviour; but onely a Power to proclaim the Kingdom of Christ, and to perswade men to submit themselves thereunto; and by precepts and good counsell, to teach them that have submitted, what they are to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by scriptural metaphors (fishing, leaven, seed) and the name 'Regeneration' — ministers are 'Fishers of Men' and evangelizers, not commanders. Hence disputes about ecclesiastical monarchy/aristocracy are vain if they claim coercive, sovereign, or punitive authority solely from Christ's commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ's kingdom not of this world; reign begins at the Resurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kingdome of Christ is not to be before the Son of Man shall come in Glory; his Kingdome was not to begin till the Resurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages (Mat. 19.28; Mat. 16.27; Luke 22.29–30) are cited to show apostles will judge and sit on thrones only when Christ comes in glory — present ministry is preparatory, not reign in majesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ's earthly authority is subordinate to the Father
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ, whose authority, as man, was to bee like that of Moses, was no more but subordinate to the authority of his Father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies to Moses, high priests, and the scriptural liturgy ('For thine is the Kingdome, the power and the Glory') are used to show Christ (in his human office) rules as viceregent and must ultimately deliver the kingdom up to the Father (1 Cor. 15.24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical authority is transmitted by imposition of hands (apostolic succession)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposition of hands... was signified the giving of the Holy Spirit, or Spirit of God, to those whom they ordained Ministers of God, to advance his Kingdome. So that Imposition of hands, was nothing else but the Seal of their Commission to Preach Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallels drawn from Moses laying hands on Joshua (Deut. 34.9) and Christ breathing on the apostles (John 20.22) and Pentecost (Acts 2). The page treats succession by laying on of hands as the means by which ecclesiastical power continued in apostles' successors.

rubrics_metrics.name: The power ecclesiastical is essentially the power to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: The Power Ecclesiasticall Is But The Power To Teach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preachers are described as schoolmasters, not commanders; their precepts are 'wholesome Counsells' rather than laws. This is argued as decisive against claims that ministers hold sovereign coercive powers from Christ alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers cannot require civil obedience in Christ's name absent civil authority
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Supreme King have not his Regall Power in this world; by what authority can obedience be required to his Officers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Christ's non-regal present status implies his ministers lack the title-based authority to compel obedience. Only when ministers also hold civil sovereign power (through political institution) may they lawfully punish or command in temporal matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith cannot be compelled; ministers have no power to punish unbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith hath no relation to, nor dependence at all upon Compulsion, or Commandement; but onely upon certainty, or probability of Arguments... therefore the Ministers of Christ in this world, have no Power by that title, to Punish any man for not Beleeving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 2 Cor. 1.24 'Wee have no Dominion over your Faith, but are Helpers of your Joy.' The nature of faith as internally convinced by reason or testimony excludes coercion as a means to produce genuine belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to obey civil rulers even if they are infidels
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit your selves to every Ordinance of Man... whether it bee to the King, as Supreme, or unto Governours, as to them that be sent by him for the punishment of evill doers... for so is the will of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Romans 13, 1 Peter 2, Titus 3 and emphasizes that civil authority is ordained by God and must be obeyed; ministers' spiritual mission does not justify disobedience to lawful sovereigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of outward dissimulation under compulsion (to avoid persecution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Profession with the tongue is but an externall thing... a Christian, holding firmely in his heart the Faith of Christ, hath the same liberty which the Prophet Elisha allowed to Naaman the Syrian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Naaman's example (2 Kings 5.17) and reasoning about the subject's obedience to a sovereign, the text permits outward compliance (even apparent denial) when compelled by lawful civil authority to avoid death — the action is attributable to the sovereign, not the subject's conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Martyr — narrow and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: A Martyr is... a Witnesse of the Resurrection of Jesus the Messiah; which none can be but those that conversed with him on earth, and saw him after he was risen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only original disciples who had direct experience of Christ and his resurrection qualify as primary martyrs; others are 'second martyrs' (martyrs of the witnesses). Dying for non-fundamental doctrines or for clergy ambition/profit does not merit the name 'martyr.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolic commission confers preaching, teaching, baptizing, and binding/loosing, not magisterial sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: The points of their Commission, as they are expressely set down in the Gospel, contain none of them any authority over the Congregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four enumerated functions are considered ministerial: to Preach (proclaim), to Teach (reason from Scripture), to Baptize (sign of reception), and to Forgive/Retain sins (keys). None of these, by themselves, constitute the right to command civil obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preaching is proclamation (herald/crying), not a claim to command
rubrics_metrics.description: Preaching in the originall, is that act, which a Crier, Herald, or other Officer useth to doe publiquely in Proclaiming of a King. But a Crier hath not right to Command any man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preachers are ministers, not 'Masters' with magisterial authority; Luke 10 and Matthew 20 are cited to stress ministerial, servant office ('not as Lords of the Harvest').

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching (reasoning from Scripture) persuades but does not permit disobedience to civil law
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching... is to make known by what right [Christ] commeth, if they mean men shall submit themselves unto him... but to teach out of the Old Testament that Jesus was Christ... is not to say, that men are bound after they beleeve it, to obey those that tell them so, against the laws, and commands of their Soveraigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paul's example in Thessalonica (reasoning three sabbath days) shows teaching aims at persuasion and preparation, not at issuing commands that conflict with civil duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baptism as sign of new birth and pledge of allegiance, not creation of temporal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Baptisme... is Dipped or Washed, as a sign of becomming a new man, and a loyall subject to that God... This, being our promise in Baptisme; and the Authority of Earthly Soveraigns being not to be put down till the day of Judgment... it is manifest, that we do not in Baptisme constitute over us another authority, by which our externall actions are to be governed in this life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baptism admits into the Kingdom of God (remission of sins) but does not supplant or grant civil/regulative authority over subjects' temporal actions while civil sovereignty remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to remit and retain sins (the keys) is conditional and tied to baptismal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Power of Remission, And Retention Of Sinnes... is a consequence of the Authority to Baptize, or refuse to Baptize... By which words, is not granted an Authority to Forgive, or Retain Sins, simply and absolutely... but conditionally, to the Penitent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolution/retention depend on outward marks of repentance; if repentance is feigned the absolution is void. Apostles/pastors follow external signs; the assembly judges the truth of repentance (Mat. 18), while sentence is pronounced by an apostle or pastor (1 Cor. 5 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment about the truth of repentance belongs to the Church assembly; sentence to the apostle/pastor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judgment concerning the truth of Repentance, belonged not to any one Man, but to the Church, that is, to the Assembly of the Faithfull... but the Sentence therefore by which a man was put out of the Church, was pronounced by the Apostle, or Pastor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mat. 18:15–17 establishes procedure: private admonition, witnesses, then assembly. The assembly assesses merit; the apostle/pastor pronounces binding sentences (e.g., to cast out).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication defined as casting out of the congregation/synagogue
rubrics_metrics.description: To excommunicate, is in the Originall, Aposunagogon Poiein, To Cast Out Of The Synagogue; that is, out of the place of Divine service; a word drawn from the custom of the Jews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term derives from Jewish practice of separating contagious manners/doctrine (like lepers). It means exclusion from assemblies and divine service rather than necessarily civil penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of excommunication without civil power: social avoidance, not civil penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: The Use and Effect of Excommunication, whilest it was not yet strengthened with the Civill Power, was no more, than that they, who were not Excommunicate, were to avoid the company of them that were.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excommunicated persons were to be avoided socially (not to eat with them, etc.). They could still enter places by civil commission; keeping them out of synagogues depended on the owner's or magistrate's authority. Thus, absent civil enforcement, excommunication's worldly effects were limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication has no worldly effect on apostates under persecuting civil regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon a Christian, that should become an Apostate, in a place where the Civill Power did persecute, or not assist the Church, the effect of Excommunication had nothing in it, neither of dammage in this world, nor of terrour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When civil powers reward apostasy or persecute the Church, excommunication loses its temporal deterrent; apostates may re-enter worldly favour and suffer no greater worldly harm than non-believers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trinity explained as three 'persons' by representation over time
rubrics_metrics.description: God... was the Person Represented by Moses; the Person Represented by his Son Incarnate; and the Person Represented by the Apostles... God... may properly enough be said to be three Persons; though neither the word Person, nor Trinity be ascribed to him in the Bible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'person' as a relative to a representer: plurality of representers (Moses, Son, Apostles) yields plurality of 'Persons' though one substance; ties theological language to historical representation rather than metaphysical divisions.
